stages.label: Things stop moving
stages.what: Goods are moving more slowly through rail, ports or sea lanes.

chains.title: Fertilizer imports are cut before seeding
chains.summary: A closed route or a trade dispute raises world fertilizer prices first, then what Canadian farmers pay, then next year's crops.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.

watch.why: About a third of the world's seaborne fertilizer trade normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so fewer ships there is an early sign.
watch.title: Ships through key sea lanes
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: Ships through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 3 a day over the four weeks to 22 November 2026. In the same weeks of the past five years the typical figure was about 83 a day. That is below the range of every one of those years, about 96% below the typical level. Also unusual: Bab el-Mandeb Strait (fewer ships than usual).

watch.why: World fertilizer prices move within weeks of a supply disruption, well before Canadian farmers buy.
watch.title: World fertilizer prices
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: In October 2026, the World Bank's fertilizer price index stood at 148 (2010 = 100), 6% higher than a year earlier. Prices: DAP US$803 a tonne; Urea US$420 a tonne. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year, in US dollars without adjusting for inflation. It is about 8% below the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year. Across all the series in this group, one is outside the range of past years.

stages.label: Things stop moving
stages.what: Goods are moving more slowly through rail, ports or sea lanes.

watch.why: Potash and other fertilizer move by rail; a fall means less is reaching dealers.
watch.title: Grain and fertilizer moved by rail
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: Railways carried 3.8 million tonnes of wheat, other grains and canola in August 2026. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 80% above the typical level. It is rising much faster than usual for this time of year. Both checks agree, so this one is worth a closer look.

watch.why: Imported fertilizer arrives through the same ports as grain leaves.
watch.title: Cargo loaded at Canadian ports
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: Ships loaded an estimated 1.6 million tonnes a week at the Port of Vancouver in the four weeks to 20 November 2026. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 11% above the typical level. Elsewhere, unusual: Prince Rupert (less than usual). Across all the series in this group, one is outside the range of past years.

stages.label: Stored supply is used up
stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: What Canadian farmers actually pay. This is the point at which a world price becomes a Canadian cost.
watch.title: What farmers pay for inputs
watch.rung_label: Moving unusually fast, but still within past years
watch.text: In the quarter starting April 2026, the prices Canadian farmers paid for all inputs stood at 187 on Statistics Canada's index (2020 = 100), 11% higher than a year earlier. Fertilizer alone was 24% higher. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 20% above the typical level. It is rising a little faster than usual for this time of year, but not enough to stand out. A new high or low on a figure that climbs year after year is the normal state, not a warning: it is the pace that would make it one. Across all the series in this group, three of the four are moving unusually fast and one is outside the range of past years.

watch.why: Fertilizer is priced in US dollars, so a weaker Canadian dollar adds to the cost even when the world price is flat.
watch.title: The Canadian dollar
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: One US dollar cost $1.42 Canadian on average so far in November 2026, 1.0% more than a year earlier. A weaker Canadian dollar makes imported food and farm inputs dearer. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 4% above the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year. A new high or low on a figure that climbs year after year is the normal state, not a warning: it is the pace that would make it one.

stages.label: It reaches people
stages.what: Prices in shops, or what people can afford, have moved.

watch.why: A fertilizer shock reaches shops a season later, through smaller crops, if at all.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: We follow 15 everyday foods in Canadian stores. In September 2026, two cost more and three cost less than in the same month of any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. Higher than usual: ground beef, whole chicken. Across all the series in this group, one of the 15 set off both checks.

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: A sea lane closing or world fertilizer prices rising unusually fast. There is usually a season between this and seeding.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: What farmers pay rising unusually fast, or the dollar weakening on top of it. Alternative supply takes about eight weeks to reach farms, so this is the last useful moment.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Shop prices moving. By this point the crop has already been grown with whatever fertilizer was available.

depends_on.assumption: The farm input price index shows what farmers are paying now.
depends_on.would_change: It is published every three months, and many farmers book fertilizer months ahead at a price fixed then. So the index can stay flat while next spring's cost is already set, and it can rise after the decisions that mattered have been taken.

depends_on.assumption: Ship counts at the Strait of Hormuz stand in for fertilizer supply reaching world markets.
depends_on.would_change: The counts do not say what the ships carry. If fertilizer found another route, transits could stay low while supply recovered.

chains.text: The readings along this chain have reached the stage “stored supply is used up”: 1 of the 2 figures we watch there is saying so. Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move. On the team's judgement that matches the “get ready” sign below.

chains.title: The main rail line to Vancouver closes
chains.summary: A closed rail corridor first stops grain moving, then fills the elevators behind it, then empties the plants and shops in front of it.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.

watch.why: A strike or lockout under way is how most rail closures start.
watch.title: Strikes and lockouts
watch.rung_label: Nothing unusual in these readings
watch.text: There were 74 strikes and lockouts under way in Canada in September 2026, three of them in transportation. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 34% above the typical level.

watch.why: Trucking is the fallback when rail stops, and its cost sets how much of that is affordable.
watch.title: Diesel prices
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: Diesel at self-serve pumps averaged 262.9 cents a litre across five cities in October 2026, 71% more than a year earlier. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 51% above the typical level. It is rising much faster than usual for this time of year. Both checks agree, so this one is worth a closer look.

stages.label: Things stop moving
stages.what: Goods are moving more slowly through rail, ports or sea lanes.

watch.why: Fewer tonnes loaded onto railways is the most direct sign that the corridor is not working.
watch.title: Grain and fertilizer moved by rail
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: Railways carried 3.8 million tonnes of wheat, other grains and canola in August 2026. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 80% above the typical level. It is rising much faster than usual for this time of year. Both checks agree, so this one is worth a closer look.

watch.why: Grain leaving port terminals falls within days of a corridor closing.
watch.title: Grain shipped through ports
watch.late_note: The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.
watch.rung_label: Moving unusually fast, but still within past years
watch.text: Ports shipped 3.21 million tonnes of grain abroad in the four weeks to 4 October 2026. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 4% above the typical level. It is falling much faster than usual for this time of year. It has not yet passed the range of past years, so this is the earlier of the two signals. The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.

watch.why: Cargo loaded at Vancouver and Prince Rupert falls when nothing arrives by rail.
watch.title: Cargo loaded at Canadian ports
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: Ships loaded an estimated 1.6 million tonnes a week at the Port of Vancouver in the four weeks to 20 November 2026. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 11% above the typical level. Elsewhere, unusual: Prince Rupert (less than usual). Across all the series in this group, one is outside the range of past years.

stages.label: Stored supply is used up
stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: Grain piling up in elevators is the sign of a blockage, not of a comfortable reserve. Read it with the shipment figures: high stocks and low shipments together mean grain that cannot move.
watch.title: Grain in storage
watch.late_note: The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: Grain elevators and port terminals held 7.25 million tonnes of grain in the week ending 4 October 2026. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 2% above the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year. A new high or low on a figure that climbs year after year is the normal state, not a warning: it is the pace that would make it one. The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.

watch.why: Processors drawing down stock faster than usual means what they need is not arriving.
watch.title: Stock held by food processors
watch.rung_label: Nothing unusual in these readings
watch.text: In September 2026, food processors held about $0.98 of stock for every dollar of food they shipped that month. Of that, $0.54 was finished food ready to ship. Across all manufacturing the figure was $1.55. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 4% below the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year.

stages.label: It reaches people
stages.what: Prices in shops, or what people can afford, have moved.

watch.why: Shelf prices are the last thing to move, and the slowest.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: We follow 15 everyday foods in Canadian stores. In September 2026, two cost more and three cost less than in the same month of any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. Higher than usual: ground beef, whole chicken. Across all the series in this group, one of the 15 set off both checks.

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: A strike notice, a flood warning or an unusual rise in trucking costs. At this point the corridor is still working.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: Rail tonnes, port cargo or grain shipments falling unusually fast. This is where moving food, feed and fertilizer first, and booking trucks and other ports, still changes the outcome.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Elevators filling while shipments stay low, or processors drawing down stock. By here the damage is already being done and the response is about limiting it.

depends_on.assumption: Monthly rail tonnes are the best available measure of whether the corridor is working.
depends_on.would_change: They arrive about two months after the month ends, so a closure that starts and finishes inside a month may never appear. A sharp fall in port cargo or grain shipments, which are weekly, would reach this chain first.

depends_on.assumption: Grain piling up in commercial elevators means a blockage rather than a good harvest.
depends_on.would_change: A large harvest raises stocks for a reason that has nothing to do with transport. If stocks rise while shipments stay normal, this stage should not be read as a blockage.

chains.text: The readings along this chain have reached the stage “stored supply is used up”: 1 of the 2 figures we watch there is saying so. Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move. On the team's judgement that matches the “act now” sign below. Every figure putting it there is older than its source normally publishes, so this is where the chain stood when the data stopped, not where it stands today. Check the sources before treating it as current. Some of the figures behind “things stop moving, stored supply is used up” are older than their source normally publishes, so read this as the last position we could measure, not the current one.

chains.title: Bird flu reaches a major poultry region
chains.summary: An outbreak kills birds and closes export markets, then shows up as fewer eggs and birds, then as prices.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.
stages.unwatched_why: Canada has no current, openly licensed count of infected premises. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency's reportable terrestrial animal disease dataset is published under the Open Government Licence but stops in 2021, so there is nothing to read here. Its announcements appear under the current warnings, with their headline, date and link only.

stages.label: Stored supply is used up
stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: Processors drawing down stock is the first measurable sign that supply has been interrupted, though it covers all food and not poultry alone.
watch.title: Stock held by food processors
watch.rung_label: Nothing unusual in these readings
watch.text: In September 2026, food processors held about $0.98 of stock for every dollar of food they shipped that month. Of that, $0.54 was finished food ready to ship. Across all manufacturing the figure was $1.55. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 4% below the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year.

stages.label: It reaches people
stages.what: Prices in shops, or what people can afford, have moved.

watch.why: The price of a dozen eggs is the most direct published reading of a poultry supply shock.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods: Eggs, 1 dozen
watch.rung_label: Nothing unusual in these readings

watch.why: Whole chicken, for the same reason.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods: Whole chicken, per kilogram
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: A first detection near a dense poultry region. We cannot currently see this in data; it would come from the agency's own announcements.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: Processor stocks falling. Movement controls and surge surveillance still change the outcome at this point.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Egg and chicken prices moving in shops. The birds have already been lost.

evidence.title: Store prices for everyday foods: Whole chicken, per kilogram

depends_on.assumption: Egg and chicken prices in shops reflect a poultry supply shock.
depends_on.would_change: They are national monthly averages published about six weeks later, and supply-managed pricing dampens and delays the signal. A regional outbreak could run its course without moving them at all. This chain is weakly watched and should be read that way.

chains.text: Nothing has travelled along this chain: the earliest stage we can read is quiet. A reading further down the chain, at “it reaches people”, has also moved — but nothing upstream of it has, so this chain is not the explanation. Look for another cause, such as prices across the board. We have no figure at all for the stage “pressure from outside”, so a shock could be under way there and this chain would stay quiet.

chains.title: A cyberattack takes a grocery distributor offline
chains.summary: An outage empties shelves within days, drawing down whatever stock sits behind them.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.
stages.unwatched_why: There is no public feed that confirms an outage at a named food business. Cyber advisories describe vulnerabilities, not incidents, and companies rarely disclose quickly. This stage is unwatched by necessity.

stages.label: Stored supply is used up
stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: Stock held between plants and shops is what an outage eats into, though a month-end national figure may miss an outage lasting a week.
watch.title: Stock held by food processors
watch.rung_label: Nothing unusual in these readings
watch.text: In September 2026, food processors held about $0.98 of stock for every dollar of food they shipped that month. Of that, $0.54 was finished food ready to ship. Across all manufacturing the figure was $1.55. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 4% below the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year.

stages.label: It reaches people
stages.what: Prices in shops, or what people can afford, have moved.

watch.why: A short outage is more likely to empty shelves than to move average prices, so this stage may stay quiet even in a serious incident.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: We follow 15 everyday foods in Canadian stores. In September 2026, two cost more and three cost less than in the same month of any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. Higher than usual: ground beef, whole chicken. Across all the series in this group, one of the 15 set off both checks.

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: A reported outage at a major distributor. We cannot see this in data.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: Stock between plants and shops falling unusually fast. Manual ordering and mutual aid still work at this point.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Prices moving. Shelves will have been empty for some days already.

depends_on.assumption: Stock held by food processors stands in for the buffer between plants and shops.
depends_on.would_change: It measures dollars at the end of a month across the whole country, so a one-week outage at one distributor would very likely not appear. Treat a quiet reading here as no evidence, not as evidence of nothing.

chains.text: Nothing has travelled along this chain: the earliest stage we can read is quiet. We have no figure at all for the stage “pressure from outside”, so a shock could be under way there and this chain would stay quiet.

chains.title: A severe drought hits the Prairies
chains.summary: Dry soil reduces the crop and the hay, which empties feed stores, which forces herd sales and lifts prices.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.

watch.why: The share of Prairie farmland in moderate drought or worse, from the Canadian Drought Monitor.
watch.title: Drought on the Prairies
watch.rung_label: Not enough past data to compare
watch.text: At the end of October 2026, 37% of southern Alberta, 0% of southern Saskatchewan and 25% of southern Manitoba were in moderate drought or worse. In Alberta, the province with the most drought, it is inside the range of the past three years for this time of year. It is about 52% below the typical level.

watch.why: Drought in California, Arizona, Florida and Washington affects the fruit and vegetables Canada imports, so a dry year on both sides leaves fewer alternatives.
watch.title: Drought where imported produce grows
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: In the week of 17 November 2026, 9% of California; 9% of Arizona; 7% of Florida; 59% of Washington was in moderate drought or worse. Unusual for the time of year: Arizona (less drought than in any of the past five years). Across all the series in this group, one is outside the range of past years.

stages.label: Stored supply is used up
stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: A smaller harvest shows up as less grain in store, with a lag of months.
watch.title: Grain in storage
watch.late_note: The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: Grain elevators and port terminals held 7.25 million tonnes of grain in the week ending 4 October 2026. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 2% above the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year. A new high or low on a figure that climbs year after year is the normal state, not a warning: it is the pace that would make it one. The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.

watch.why: The only reading that includes grain on farms, which is where feed grain is held.
watch.title: All grain in the country, farms included
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
watch.text: At the end of July 2026, Canada held 6.6 million tonnes of wheat in total, counting grain on farms as well as in elevators and at ports. About 38% of it was still on farms. Elevators and port terminals held 4.1 million tonnes. It is the highest of the six comparable readings: this one and the past five years. It is about 25% above the typical level. Worth a closer look. One reading does not mean a crisis.

stages.label: It reaches people
stages.what: Prices in shops, or what people can afford, have moved.

watch.why: Wholesale fruit and vegetable prices respond to drought where the food is grown, including abroad.
watch.title: Fresh fruit and vegetable prices
watch.rung_label: Moving unusually fast, but still within past years
watch.text: We follow 12 fresh fruits and vegetables at the Toronto wholesale market. In the latest week, two cost more and two cost less than at this time of year in any recent year, after allowing for inflation. Four are in their normal range, and for four we do not have enough past data. Four of the 12 are also rising or falling unusually fast, but no product sets off both checks at once.

watch.why: Shop prices follow a drought by a season or more, mostly through meat and dairy.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods
watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast
watch.text: We follow 15 everyday foods in Canadian stores. In September 2026, two cost more and three cost less than in the same month of any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. Higher than usual: ground beef, whole chicken. Across all the series in this group, one of the 15 set off both checks.

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: Moderate drought or worse on the Drought Monitor during the growing season. Sourcing feed now is cheap; sourcing it in August is not.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: Grain and feed stocks falling unusually fast or unusually low. Feed takes about a month to arrive once it is ordered.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Prices moving in shops and at wholesale. Herd sales have usually already happened.

depends_on.assumption: The share of each Prairie province south of 54 degrees north in drought stands in for the share of its farmland in drought.
depends_on.would_change: The areas measured are straight-sided boxes that include forest, lakes and towns, and the monitor's archive starts in 2023, so there are at most three years to compare and this reading cannot set off the level check on its own. A crop-area mask would change both.

depends_on.assumption: Falling grain stocks after a dry summer reflect a smaller harvest.
depends_on.would_change: Strong exports empty the same elevators for the opposite reason. Read the shipment figures alongside: stocks falling while shipments are high is a good year, not a bad one.

chains.text: Nothing has travelled along this chain: the earliest stage we can read is quiet. Some of the figures behind “stored supply is used up” are older than their source normally publishes, so read this as the last position we could measure, not the current one.

chains.title: A major buyer closes its market
chains.summary: A lost market first stops shipments, then fills storage, then cuts farm incomes. Shop prices may not move at all.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.

watch.why: A trade dispute usually moves the currency before it moves the cargo.
watch.title: The Canadian dollar
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace

A new high or low on a figure that climbs year after year is the normal state, not a warning: it is the pace that would make it one.

watch.rung_label: Outside past years and moving unusually fast

stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: Grain that cannot be sold stays in store.
watch.title: Grain in storage
watch.late_note: The Canadian Grain Commission normally publishes weekly, but has published nothing since 4 October 2026, 52 days ago. This is the last figure it published, not a current one.

watch.why: When commercial elevators are full, the grain stays on farms.
watch.title: All grain in the country, farms included
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: A trade action threatened, with the currency or world prices moving. Finding other buyers is far easier before the duty takes effect.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: Shipments and port cargo falling. Redirecting sales and financing storage still helps here.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Storage filling up. From here farmers are choosing between selling cheaply and paying to store.

evidence.title: All grain in the country, farms included

depends_on.assumption: A fall in grain leaving port terminals reflects lost sales.
depends_on.would_change: A rail or port problem produces exactly the same fall. If the rail chain is also showing movement, the cause is more likely transport than trade.

chains.text: Nothing has travelled along this chain: the earliest stage we can read is quiet. A reading further down the chain, at “things stop moving”, “stored supply is used up”, has also moved — but nothing upstream of it has, so this chain is not the explanation. Look for another cause, such as prices across the board. Some of the figures behind “things stop moving, stored supply is used up” are older than their source normally publishes, so read this as the last position we could measure, not the current one.

chains.title: Illness spreads through meat-plant workers
chains.summary: Absence closes processing lines, which backs animals up on farms and thins the meat counter.

stages.label: Pressure from outside
stages.what: A cost, a price or a supply route outside the chain has moved.
stages.unwatched_why: There is no current public reading of absence at food plants. Public health reporting covers communities, not workplaces, and Statistics Canada's work absence figures are annual and industry-wide.

stages.label: Stored supply is used up
stages.what: Stocks are being drawn down, or are piling up because they cannot move.

watch.why: Stock falling while shipments hold up is what a processing slowdown looks like in published data.
watch.title: Stock held by food processors
watch.rung_label: Nothing unusual in these readings
watch.text: In September 2026, food processors held about $0.98 of stock for every dollar of food they shipped that month. Of that, $0.54 was finished food ready to ship. Across all manufacturing the figure was $1.55. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 4% below the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year.

stages.label: It reaches people
stages.what: Prices in shops, or what people can afford, have moved.

watch.why: Ground beef is the most widely bought meat and the first to move.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods: Ground beef, per kilogram
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace

watch.why: Whole chicken, for the same reason.
watch.title: Store prices for everyday foods: Whole chicken, per kilogram
watch.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace

signs.label: Watch
signs.text: Community cases rising near major plants. We cannot see this in data.

signs.label: Get ready
signs.text: Processor stocks falling unusually fast. Protections and staffing changes still help here.

signs.label: Act now
signs.text: Meat prices moving in shops. Lines have already been running short.

evidence.title: Store prices for everyday foods: Ground beef, per kilogram
Store prices for everyday foods: Whole chicken, per kilogram

depends_on.assumption: Falling processor stocks reflect lines running below capacity.
depends_on.would_change: Stocks also fall when demand is strong and everything is working. Read it with the price readings: stocks falling while prices are flat is a busy month, not a shortage.

chains.text: Nothing has travelled along this chain: the earliest stage we can read is quiet. A reading further down the chain, at “it reaches people”, has also moved — but nothing upstream of it has, so this chain is not the explanation. Look for another cause, such as prices across the board. We have no figure at all for the stage “pressure from outside”, so a shock could be under way there and this chain would stay quiet.

note: Each chain shows how far along the food chain the published readings have reached. The stages and the levels that count as a reading speaking are the research team's judgement, not measurements, and no Canadian threshold for any of them has been validated against past events. The readings themselves are published figures, and each one is named so it can be checked. This is not a forecast and not a warning: only the responsible agency can issue a warning.
